passage:
Pankaj Veerji,
I'm writing because every time I try to say this aloud, we end up shouting.
For a year now your drinking has grown. I've watched you miss Sunday lunch, forget Bebe's birthday, and come home at three banging the gate. I've lied to the neighbours for you. I'm worried sick, I'm angry, and honestly I'm ashamed of how often I cover for you. I'm also exhausted.
I can't make you stop. I know that now. But I can decide what I do. I won't lie for you any more. I won't give you money. I won't get in the car when you've been drinking.
I've started going to a support group for families on Thursdays, and it helps me. If you ever want help, I'll come with you anywhere.
I love you. That's why I'm writing.
Amandeep

qa.q: On which day does Amandeep go to the support group?
qa.a: Amandeep goes on Thursdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Amandeep describe?
qa.a: Amandeep feels worried sick, angry, ashamed of covering for Pankaj, and exhausted.

qa.q: Which limits does Amandeep set, and why are they wise?
qa.a: No more lying for Pankaj, no money and no car rides after drinking; they protect Amandeep without trying to control Pankaj.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel defensive or hurt at first, but also see that Amandeep is writing out of love.

My name's Lalremsiami, but everyone calls me Siami. You asked why I moved out of the flat? It was Ramesh. We'd been best friends since first year. At first he smoked weed at weekends. Then every evening. Then before class. He stopped turning up for our project, borrowed money he didn't return, and got snappy if I said anything. I lay awake worrying about him, and then felt furious at him for making me worry. I was so tired.
I tried everything. Hiding his stuff. Begging. Nothing changed, because it wasn't mine to change. A counsellor at college helped me see that. So I told Ramesh: not in our flat, no more loans, and I'm here if you want help. He didn't take it well. I moved in with another friend. I still message him on Sundays. I've stopped trying to fix him, and I've started sleeping again.

qa.q: When does Lalremsiami still message Ramesh?
qa.a: Lalremsiami still messages Ramesh on Sundays.

qa.q: What feelings did Lalremsiami go through while living with Ramesh?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt worried, then furious at being made to worry, and deeply tired.

qa.q: What helped Lalremsiami, and which limits were set?
qa.a: A college counsellor helped Lalremsiami stop trying to fix Ramesh; the limits were no weed in the flat, no more loans and an open offer of help.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Lalremsiami's limits?
qa.a: Ramesh didn't take them well at first and may feel judged, though the Sunday messages show the door is still open.

passage: In the village near Muzaffarpur, Ganga, nineteen, ran a small tailoring stall from the front of the house. Her elder brother Kiran had started drinking country liquor with the other men in the evenings. Now it was most nights. He came home loud, slept past noon and asked her for money. At the well, the women whispered, and Ganga walked home with her face burning. She lay awake worrying he'd hurt himself on the road, then felt furious at him in the morning. She was exhausted. One day she went to the women's self-help group and told them. They listened. The leader said, 'You can't stop him. But you can stop paying for it, and you can look after yourself.' That evening, when Kiran asked for money, Ganga said, 'No. I love you, but no.'

qa.q: What did Ganga run from the front of the house?
qa.a: A small tailoring stall.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as the women whispered at the well?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, with her face burning, and also worried and exhausted.

qa.q: What limit did Ganga set, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She stopped giving Kiran money, which protects her and stops her from paying for his drinking.

qa.a: He may be angry or surprised at first, but it shows him his drinking has consequences.

passage: Siddiq and Ulla had shared a flat in Oslo for two years, and it used to be easy. Now Ulla was drinking most nights, sometimes alone, sometimes bringing strangers home at three. Siddiq kept finding her asleep on the bathroom floor and helping her to bed. He covered for her with the landlord. In the mornings he felt angry, then guilty for being angry, then too tired to concentrate in lectures. One night, sitting on the stairs, he realised he couldn't fix this. He went to the university counselling service the next day. They helped him think about limits. That weekend he told Ulla calmly: 'I care about you. I'm not lying to the landlord any more, and I'm not staying up every night.' He gave her the number of a support service. Then he went to bed and slept.

qa.q: How long had Siddiq and Ulla shared a flat?
qa.a: For two years.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling in the mornings?
qa.a: He felt angry, then guilty for being angry, and then exhausted.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do to protect himself?
qa.a: He went to the counselling service, set limits about lying and staying up, and gave Ulla a support number.

The counselling room at the college smelled of old files and tea. Baljeet sat on the edge of the chair, twisting a hostel key.
"It's my brother, Ramesh. He's drinking every night now. Last weekend he took the money I'd saved for books and didn't come home."
"How are you sleeping?" the counsellor asked.
"Badly. I keep my phone loud in case Mummy calls. I'm angry with him, and then ashamed of being angry. And tired. So tired."
"You can't make Ramesh stop. That part isn't yours to carry. But you can decide what you will and won't do."
Baljeet was quiet. "No more lending him anything. And I'll stop answering his calls after midnight."
"That's a fair limit. There's also a family support group here on Thursdays. Would you try one meeting?"
Baljeet nodded slowly.

qa.q: When does the family support group meet?
qa.a: On Thursdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Baljeet describe, and what shows the strain?
qa.a: Baljeet feels angry, then ashamed of the anger, and deeply tired; the twisted key and sleepless nights with a loud phone show the strain.

qa.q: What limits does Baljeet choose, and why are they wise?
qa.a: No more lending and no calls after midnight; they protect Baljeet without pretending to control Ramesh.

qa.q: How might Mummy be affected by Ramesh's drinking, judging from the passage?
qa.a: Mummy is probably worried too, since Baljeet keeps the phone loud in case she calls.

grounding: Shows a young adult affected by a brother's growing drinking feeling worry, anger, shame and exhaustion, and choosing limits and support instead of control.
